articles.body_text: Con el final de ciertas celebraciones del año, muchos trabajadores y estudiantes ya empiezan a revisar el calendario para conocer cuál será el siguiente descanso oficial del año. Los feriados representan una oportunidad para planificar viajes, compartir tiempo en familia o simplemente hacer una pausa en la rutina, por lo que existe un gran interés en conocer las próximas fechas establecidas por ley. Además de permitir un espacio para el descanso, estas jornadas suelen generar un importante movimiento en sectores como el turismo, el comercio, la gastronomía y el transporte, debido al incremento de personas que aprovechan los días libres para salir de la ciudad o realizar diversas actividades. Del mismo modo, muchas empresas y entidades organizan con anticipación sus operaciones para adecuarse al calendario oficial, mientras que las familias aprovechan estas fechas para programar reuniones, escapadas de fin de semana o visitas a distintos destinos del país. Por ello, conocer con anticipación cuándo será el próximo feriado resulta clave para organizar la agenda personal y laboral, evitar contratiempos y sacar el máximo provecho a los días de descanso que aún quedan en el 2026. A continuación, te contaremos todo lo que debes saber sobre esta situación. Si quieres saber cuándo será el próximo feriado y qué fechas aún quedan por disfrutar este año, aquí te contamos todos los detalles. Los feriados son fechas establecidas por ley en las que los trabajadores tienen derecho a suspender sus labores sin que ello afecte su remuneración. Durante estas jornadas, el descanso es obligatorio tanto para el sector público como para el privado, salvo en aquellas actividades que, por su naturaleza, deben continuar operando. Si un trabajador presta servicios durante un feriado y no recibe un día de descanso compensatorio, la legislación laboral establece que le corresponde una remuneración adicional por haber laborado en esa fecha, conforme a las disposiciones vigentes. A diferencia del feriado, el día no laborable no constituye un descanso obligatorio para todos los trabajadores. Generalmente, esta medida se aplica al sector público con el objetivo de extender periodos de descanso o promover actividades como el turismo interno. En el caso de las entidades públicas, las horas que no se trabajan deben recuperarse posteriormente, dentro del plazo fijado por la normativa o según lo disponga cada institución. Para el sector privado, la aplicación de un día no laborable depende de un acuerdo entre empleador y trabajadores. Si no existe consenso sobre la recuperación de las horas, será el empleador quien determine la forma en que estas deberán compensarse.

articles.title: Upwind raises $400M after walking away from Datadog acquisition offer | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The cloud security startup raised a Series C at a $3.8B valuation, instead of selling itself for the same price.
articles.body_text: Upwind, a San Francisco startup that uses AI to secure cloud infrastructure, has raised a $400 million Series C round at a $3.8 billion valuation led by Bessemer Venture Partners, with participation from existing backers including Greylock Partners and Craft Ventures. The round comes nine months after Upwind closed its previous $250 million financing at a $1.5 billion valuation . The fresh funding, which has been in the works for months, nearly fell apart after Datadog attempted to buy the company, according to a person familiar with Upwind. Datadog is a publicly traded company that sells tools for monitoring how software runs, known as observability. It didn’t offer a premium above the $3.8 billion valuation set by venture capital investors, the person said, so Upwind decided to stay independent. Four-year-old Upwind has grown rapidly amid rising AI-driven cybersecurity threats. The startup has been adding $20 million to $30 million in annualized recurring revenue (ARR) each quarter and is projected to end the year at roughly $90 million, according to a person familiar with Upwind’s financials. That means that VCs and Datadog valued the startup at more than 40 times its forecast ARR, a common yardstick for pricing software companies. The high multiple is also well below the 80x ARR fetched by Cyera, another fast-growing cybersecurity startup, according to TechCrunch reporting from earlier this year. Cybersecurity is poised to be the third big wave of AI software that companies will pay for after AI coding tools and customer support, Theory Ventures general partner Tomasz Tunguz recently wrote in his widely read blog. By walking away from an acquisition offer, Upwind clearly believes that the company will ultimately be worth more than the $3.8 billion that Datadog was ready to pay for it. However, given how few cybersecurity companies have gone public in recent years, an eventual sale remains the most likely outcome for the startup. Upwind continues to draw acquisition interest, according to a person familiar with the company. The startup was founded by Amiram Shachar, who sold his previous company, the cloud spend management startup Spot.io, to NetApp for $450 million. Upwind calls its approach to thwarting threats “runtime” security, which means it alerts and remedies attacks and vulnerabilities in active services in real time. articles.body_text: Apple has officially entered the touchscreen MacBook Pro era, and apparently, it wants to drain your wallet while it’s at it. articles.title: Microsoft just shared Azure's actual revenue in dollars: $33.2 billion | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Microsoft has never disclosed Azure's quarterly revenue in dollars. But for the first time, we can see just how close it is getting to besting the biggest competitor in the market, AWS.
articles.body_text: Microsoft has never disclosed Azure’s quarterly revenue in dollars. It has typically only shared a growth percentage or described revenue dollar milestones in vague ways. But on Wednesday, when it posted another record-breaking quarter , it reported that Azure brought in a healthy $33.2 billion in revenue for the July-September quarter, up 48% from a year earlier. The disclosure lets investors line up Azure’s performance more directly against Amazon Web Services and Google Cloud, whose parent companies already report cloud revenue in dollars every quarter. Alphabet, which also reported earnings on Wednesday, said Google Cloud brought in $30.7 billion in the same quarter, putting Azure slightly ahead. But Google Cloud, which also includes Google’s Workspace subscriptions, roughly doubled its revenue from a year earlier, growing about twice as fast as Azure, according to TechCrunch’s calculations. Azure, where businesses rent computing power to run applications, SaaS, and to build and run AI models, is now Microsoft’s largest and fastest-growing product line by the company’s own figures. It accounted for roughly 36% of Microsoft’s $92.3 billion in quarterly revenue. Azure’s revenue was also about $850 million more than the $32.3 billion analysts expected . Azure’s 48% growth rate also topped the 44% to 45% that Microsoft CFO Amy Hood forecast on the company’s July earnings call . Azure sits inside Agents and Infra, one of two new business segments Microsoft introduced this quarter. Microsoft previously reported three segments, Productivity and Business Processes, Intelligent Cloud, and More Personal Computing. The new Agents and Infra segment, which groups Azure with Microsoft 365’s cloud business, brought in $76.8 billion , up 25% from a year earlier. Amazon reports its earnings on Thursday. Analysts also expect its cloud, Amazon Web Services, to grow. It’s been the largest cloud since the beginning of time and no one expects Microsoft to best it right now. articles.title: Microsoft recorded $10 billion in revenue from OpenAI | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Microsoft said it made $10 billion in revenue from commercial arrangements with OpenAI, including revenue-sharing payments, in the quarter ending September 30. It underscores the still-enormous financial dependency of the partnership.
articles.body_text: Microsoft generated $10 billion in revenue from commercial arrangements with OpenAI, including revenue-sharing payments, in the quarter ended September 30, the company said in a regulatory filing on Wednesday. That represents nearly 11% of Microsoft’s total quarterly revenue of $92.3 billion, highlighting the enormous financial ties that remain between the two companies even as they increasingly compete for the same customers . (Microsoft’s financial year begins in July, making the quarter ended September 30, 2026 the first quarter of its fiscal 2027.) For the full 2026 fiscal year, revenue from OpenAI hit $24.1 billion. At its latest quarterly pace, Microsoft would pull in $40 billion annually from OpenAI-related arrangements. Microsoft also reported $7.2 billion in outstanding receivables from OpenAI at the end of September, up from $6 billion at the end of June. That money represents amounts OpenAI owes for previous transactions, not additional revenue. It’s not clear how much of Microsoft’s revenue from OpenAI came from revenue-sharing payments or Azure cloud computing services. TechCrunch has reached out for more information. In November 2025, TechCrunch reported , citing leaked documents, that Microsoft had received $865.8 million in net revenue-sharing payments from OpenAI during the first nine months of that year. OpenAI reportedly shares 20% of its revenue with Microsoft as part of a previous deal in which the software giant invested more than $13 billion in the AI startup. (Neither the AI lab nor Microsoft have publicly confirmed this percentage.) As part of an April 2026 agreement, OpenAI is on the hook to continue sharing revenue with Microsoft through 2030, subject to a cap, even as OpenAI is allowed to work with competing cloud providers. The companies began loosening the ties of their once-exclusive partnership in October 2025, when Microsoft relinquished its hold on OpenAI to give the startup more freedom to partner with other cloud providers. The tech giant reported yet another quarterly revenue record on Wednesday: $92.3 billion , a 19% increase over the year-ago quarter. Microsoft has now reported record-breaking revenue for 10 quarters in a row . This is profitable revenue, too. Microsoft reported that net income reached $36.6 billion, an increase of 32% on a GAAP basis, over the year-ago quarter. The record-breaking income was largely driven on the strength of Microsoft Cloud, which reached $63.9 billion in revenue this quarter, an increase of 30% over the year-ago quarter, Microsoft said. Microsoft has reorganized its business reporting into two basic segments: 1) Agents and Infra and 2) Devices and Consumer. On the flip side, revenue in Devices and Consumer was $15.5 billion, decreased of 3%, with Windows OEM and devices revenue falling 22% from the year-ago quarter. True, not all of Microsoft’s healthy cloud revenue can be attributed to AI. Microsoft 365 accounted for nearly $28 billion. But Azure brought in the most, at $33.2 billion. And again, not all of that is necessarily AI-related. Enterprises run all sorts of the traditional software and SaaS applications on Azure. Still, a good chunk of the revenue was from AI, because Microsoft also reported $10 billion in revenue from OpenAI . Despite branching out to AWS, Oracle, and others, OpenAI still runs a lot of its services on Microsoft’s cloud. (Anthropic runs on Azure as well.) Microsoft also said its “commercial remaining performance obligation increased 73% to $677 billion.” That represents future revenue committed under existing contracts of the AI labs. But, like all the big cloud providers, Microsoft is also spending big to prepare to deliver on those commitments. Capital expenditures topped $45.2 billion, another all-time quarterly record. articles.title: Hacker stole personnel data about thousands of Homeland Security employees, including CBP and ICE agents | TechCrunch
articles.summary: A hacker obtained personally identifiable information about more than 40,000 Homeland Security staffers, which has since been published online.
articles.body_text: Personally identifiable information belonging to thousands of U.S. Department of Homeland Security employees has been published online after a hacker stole reams of data in a previously undisclosed breach at the government department earlier this year. The breach includes names, job titles, and work contact information, such as email addresses, cell phone numbers, and office locations, of more than 40,000 people who work for the federal department, including border and immigration agents, cybersecurity staffers, and senior department officials. A hacker who goes by the handle Department of Peace claimed they obtained the data from an Okta single sign-on system used by Homeland Security to allow employees and contractors across its various agencies to log in to its central network. The Okta system also contains IT and log-in records associated with the employees’ user account, including details about which systems and internal apps they are permitted to access. More than half of the dataset — some 21,000 records — relate to employees with U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP), who work at airports and other ports of entry. The data also contains records associated with another 10,000 employees of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and its Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) unit, and just under a 1,000 employees who work at U.S. cybersecurity defense agency CISA. Thousands of additional records relate to staff who work at the department’s headquarters and its other agencies, including U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services and the Federal Protective Service. “They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs,” said Department of Peace in a note left with the data, which TechCrunch has seen. The hacker did not respond to TechCrunch’s email requesting comment and with questions about how the breach was carried out. This is the latest data breach to hit the U.S. government in recent months, following earlier hacks involving the theft of thousands of FBI agents’ personnel records and the personal information of millions of serving and former military service personnel from the Pentagon’s human resources unit . It’s also the second breach involving Homeland Security this year, after the same hacker claimed to have taken thousands of contracts between the department and the private sector, including defense contractors and surveillance vendors. The latest batch of breached data, which appears authentic, offers a rare — albeit incomplete — view into the scale and operations of Homeland Security, whose deportations, arbitrary detentions, and killings of U.S. citizens under its leadership have become a key issue for voters ahead of the upcoming U.S. midterm elections. The stolen Homeland Security data was provided to journalist and hacker maia arson crimew, who then shared a copy with DDoSecrets , a nonprofit collective that hosts leaked datasets in the public interest. TechCrunch verified a portion of the data as authentic by matching the names of several known Homeland Security employees against an offline copy of the database. The thousands of employee directory records appear to have been exfiltrated around mid-August, according to the timestamps on each person’s record. The number of leaked records is equivalent to about one-fifth of Homeland Security’s workforce, which totals around 220,000 staff . It’s unclear whether the vulnerability that allowed the breach has been fixed or if Homeland Security is aware of the data theft.

articles.title: Anthropic just launched tools to show companies what their AI spending is buying | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The frontier lab is lifting the curtain on how users spend money on its models ahead of a planned IPO.
articles.body_text: The financials Anthropic shared with investors this week suggest that its AI coding tool, Claude Code, is every bit the business success the frontier lab wanted. The company recorded an operating profit in the second quarter, and 900% net revenue retention — that is, spending from the same customers in Q3 2025 grew nine times in Q3 2026. Anthropic has focused on getting enterprise users to stick around and Wednesday announced a new suite of reporting tools designed to give those customers a more granular understanding of the value they get from their token spend. Using internal analytics and employee surveys, managers can view a team’s work over a given date range, what the team produced, how much it cost, and where its workflows broke down. Anthropic says it won’t use this data for model training by default. The reports will also offer recommendations on how to improve the results. This is a clear attempt to demonstrate the return on investment of Anthropic’s tools and to show customers how to improve it — a major concern among large customers. Anthropic is also creating pooled group budgets to allow teams to better manage token spending. Businesses have been hunting for that kind of information as they figure out how best to deploy AI tools. While usage among venture-backed firms is driving token spend, most of the Fortune 500 are not seeing major gains from deploying AI. Jellyfish, a company that makes tools for software developers, released a new report yesterday based on the use of agentic coding tools by 276,000 of its customers. Claude Code and other tools built on Anthropic models remain the most widely used in the survey, responsible for nearly a third of all proposed code changes submitted for review. More importantly, spending on those tools has grown 10x since the beginning of the year, with their cost now equal to about 2% of total engineering cost. “Even if you’re saying 2% is still small, that 10x growth is growth that most CFOs didn’t plan for,” Nicholas Arcolano, the chief scientist at Jellyfish, told TechCrunch. We’re certainly getting to the point where people are realizing, okay, it’s not enough to just spend a bunch. You now have to optimize it, make it work.” Anthropic’s new reports speak to that challenge. Anthropic leads among enterprise customers, but what makes an agentic coding tool truly sticky is difficult to identify. The release of OpenAI’s Astra model this summer seemed like a potential threat to Anthropic, but so far it hasn’t slowed Anthropic’s adoption numbers. “It took a long time for us to see Codex really pop in our data at all, and it has come up with Astra [OpenAI’s latest model],” Nikolas Albarran, the AI product lead at Jellyfish, told TechCrunch. Looking at X, he continued, you’d get the distinct impression that the competition is more heated. “Everyone in the Valley is like, ‘Oh, Codex is better.’” In reality, Albarran continued, “Anthropic was just there with great enterprise motions, and they had an incumbent weight of their own — this stuff just worked and worked well, and a lot of people just put a lot of effort into standardizing workflows around it. And there’s not a big enough reason to switch.” It’s not just a question of models and workflows, either. The realities of business mean that once a frontier lab has gotten its hooks into a customer, switching is harder than it is compared to an individual programmer or small organization. Albarran points to the investment all the major AI labs are making in forward-deployed engineering (FDE) organizations, teams that embed AI consultants inside customer organizations to help them get off the ground. These new reporting tools can be seen as a kind of FDE-lite, a lighter version of that hands-on help, for Anthropic customers. “We’re at a point now where it’s mature enough, where once you’re in, it’s going to be harder and harder to switch because you’ve spent the effort,” he said. “Even if they’re all mostly the same, they’re all going to be slightly different, have their own slight quirks of how they handle agent.md files, etc., and so that cost to switch is not zero.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . articles.title: Apple launches its new touchscreen MacBook Pro | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Apple's new touchscreen MacBook Pro starts at $2,899.
articles.body_text: After years of resisting, Apple today launched a MacBook Pro with a touchscreen starting at $2,899. The release comes nearly 10 years after the company first tried integrating touchscreens on its laptops, with its Touch Bar on a MacBook Pro , which it later went on to remove . The new MacBook Pro more fully embraces the touchscreen, offering a new PROLED XDR Display in both 14-inch and 16-inch screen sizes. The device is powered by M5 Pro and M5 Max chips as options to choose from, along with up to 128GB of unified memory and up to 16TB of storage. The display has 2,000 nits peak HDR and SDR brightness and a 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio. To make the new MacBook easy to use, Apple designed a hinge that stabilizes the screen when users touch it. This also helps to stabilize the camera when you are on a video call and trying to access content on the display. In addition, the screen will include a Dynamic Island-style cutout instead of the notch that’s present on most of the current MacBooks. Plus, the new MacBook features a six-speaker array with a new woofer design for better sound. The 14-inch Pro weighs 3.0 pounds (1.38 kg), and the 16-inch Pro weighs 4.0 pounds (1.82 kg) — lighter than its non-touch predecessors. Both feature three Thunderbolt 5 ports, an HDMI port, an SDXC card slot, MagSafe, and a headphone jack. Users can hook up three external displays on the M5 Pro variant and up to four displays on the M5 Max variant. The Touchscreen MacBook Pro 14-inch starts at $2,899, and the 16-inch version starts at $3,399. Consumers can place a preorder for the new touchscreen MacBook Pro from October 30, and the device will be available starting November 6. The new Touchscreen MacBook marks two marquee product launches for new CEO John Ternus, who also introduced the company’s first foldable, the iPhone Duo, in September . Various Apple executives, including Steve Jobs and Tim Cook, have scoffed at the idea of a touchscreen Mac in the past. Jobs famously called the idea “ergonomically terrible” at one point. However, rumors of the company working on such a variant started circulating nearly three years before today’s introduction . The launch follows yesterday’s unveiling of a new standard MacBook Pro with the M6 chip in 14-inch size starting from $1,999 . articles.title: AI execs may be too out of touch to build for the general public | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Tech leaders are flaunting how out of touch they are when they brag about using AI to connect with their families.
articles.body_text: Former Yahoo CEO and early Google engineer Marissa Mayer is catching a lot of flak for how she uses AI. In an interview about her new app Dazzle , an AI assistant that learns from your camera roll, Mayer poses what she believes is an impressive flex for the product: It helped her come up with three bullet points about her 10-year-old daughter for a birthday presentation at school, describing her as “empathetic, creative, and an animal lover.” It’s a vague description, like a generic horoscope — it could probably describe a lot of 10-year-olds. Some onlookers, like progressive activist Leah Greenberg, marveled that “the fact that Marissa Mayer would voluntarily disclose this to a reporter is a pretty good demonstration of how deeply the culture of Silicon Valley has diverged from the rest of humanity.” "She thought it was perfect."www.nytimes.com/2026/10/25/s… Perhaps Mayer drew so much backlash because we have repeatedly observed sheltered billionaires suggest that we outsource child-rearing — one of life’s greatest tests of patience, humility, and kindness — to a computer that is incapable of understanding human emotion. We’ve been primed for this frustration. Last year, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman told Bored Ape owner and late night host Jimmy Fallon on national television, “I cannot imagine … figuring out how to raise a newborn without ChatGPT.” The public didn’t love that comment, either, but Altman wasn’t fazed by the negative feedback. A few months ago, he said on X that a “ cool use case ” of ChatGPT Work would be creating a podcast that talks about your kids’ upcoming birthdays or soccer games and “explain[s] your kids’ interests.” (He was brutally ratioed with comments like, “What if you just talked to your children?”) After publication, Mayer defended herself in a long X post . She claims she was not relying on Dazzle to explain her child to her, but rather, she was testing what her prototype could do — it resurfaced photos of “forgotten kindergarten projects,” like a “snake devenomer” or “sandcat playground,” illustrating her daughter’s creativity and care for animals. Fair enough. But Mayer remarks in the same interview that people could also use her AI to outsource the mental load of “figuring out the theme for your child’s birthday party.” She says she’s used her app to plan a playdate for her daughter, book family activities on vacation, and decide what to be for Halloween. She even proposes that her AI assistant could coordinate plans with her husband’s AI assistant. When the reporter asks her if it’s depressing to imagine this “frictionless future … planned by AI,” Mayer replies, “I haven’t really thought that through.” These leaders seem to write off the naysayers as part of a small, angry fringe group. Yet a Pew Research Center study reports that 50% of U.S. adults think that AI will reduce people’s ability to form meaningful relationships. Only 5% of respondents said AI would make it easier to build these connections. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, however, joins his Silicon Valley kin in envisioning a world where our social needs are met via AI. “The average American I think has, it’s fewer than three friends, three people they’d consider friends, and the average person has demand for meaningfully more, I think it’s like 15 friends,” Zuckerberg said last year on a podcast . “The average person wants more connectivity, connection than they have.” Zuckerberg predicts that it will become more socially acceptable to outsource our emotional needs to AI therapists or even AI romantic partners. “There are all these things that are better about physical connections when you can have them,” he added. “But the reality is that people … feel more alone a lot of the time than they would like.”

articles.title: The Nvidia AI antitrust investigation is ‘escalating,’ reports Bloomberg
articles.summary: Nvidia and other companies have received subpoenas indicating a Department of Justice antitrust investigation into its AI chip business is moving forward.
articles.body_text: An antitrust investigation by the Department of Justice focusing on Nvidia’s AI dominance as the hardware company of choice is escalating, reports Bloomberg. The outlet reports that Nvidia and other companies have received legally binding requests for information as its sources say regulators are investigating whether Nvidia is “making it harder to switch to other suppliers and penalizes buyers that don’t exclusively use its artificial intelligence chips.” “Nvidia wins on merit, as reflected in our benchmark results and value to customers, and customers can choose whatever solution is best for them. We have inquired with the U.S. Department of Justice and have not been subpoenaed. Nonetheless, we are happy to answer any questions regulators may have about our business,” said Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo, as reported previously by CNBC. Earlier this summer, Nvidia had overtaken Microsoft as the world’s most valuable company, but now it trails both Microsoft and Apple. Before the subpoenas were reported on Tuesday afternoon, its share price dropped more than 9 percent, wiping out about $279 billion in market value in one day. But as Bloomberg notes, Nvidia’s stock is still up more than double this year as the AI boom has fueled sales of the company’s pricey chips, even after a report by The Information a few weeks ago saying that its upcoming Blackwell series of AI chips may be delayed “by three months or more due to design flaws.” Update, September 4th: Added Nvidia statement previously reported by CNBC.

articles.title: Are you being exploited by AI-powered surveillance pricing?
articles.summary: The FTC ordered Mastercard, Chase, and other companies to turn over information on their dynamic pricing products.
articles.body_text: Nearly a decade ago, Uber revealed that customers are more willing to pay surge prices when their phones are about to die. That data point sparked a pervasive belief that Uber and other ridehailing apps use algorithms to tailor each passenger’s price to their behavior and willingness to pay — a practice known as “surveillance pricing.” A related myth — that airlines use your search history to jack up prices for flights you’re interested in — is similarly ubiquitous even though it’s not true. Surveillance pricing may not be widespread yet, but experts say it’s on the horizon, and consultants are starting to offer surveillance pricing models to businesses across various industries. The Federal Trade Commission announced today that it’s ordering eight companies that offer AI surveillance pricing products and services to turn over information about the impact these pricing schemes have on privacy, competition, and consumer protection, the FTC announced today. Surveillance pricing — often called “dynamic pricing,” “personalized pricing,” or “price optimization” — involves offering individual consumers different prices for the same products based on a combination of factors, including the device they’re shopping on, their location, demographic information, credit history, and browsing and shopping history. “Firms that harvest Americans’ personal data can put people’s privacy at risk. Now firms could be exploiting this vast trove of personal information to charge people higher prices,” FTC Chair Lina Khan said in a statement. “Americans deserve to know whether businesses are using detailed consumer data to deploy surveillance pricing, and the FTC’s inquiry will shed light on this shadowy ecosystem of pricing middlemen.” Companies have already experimented with implementing Uber-style surge pricing. JetBlue quietly implemented “peak” and “off-peak” pricing to its checked bag fees in March. Walmart plans on bringing digital price tags to 2,300 stores over the next several years that will let it change products’ prices depending on a number of factors, including the weather, whether items are closer to their expiration date, and more. Wendy’s said it would roll out “dynamic pricing” in 2025. Amazon had a secret algorithm called Project Nessie that let it gauge how much it could raise its prices before its competitors took notice and changed theirs, too. [Media: https://twitter.com/TechFTC/status/1815745250649858049] These pricing models, while variable, are a bit different from surveillance pricing, which relies on using an individual consumer’s information to determine how much they’re willing to pay for a specific product. The FTC orders were sent to Mastercard, Revionics, Bloomreach, Chase, Task, Pros, Accenture, and McKinsey & Co., the FTC announced in a press release. They were issued under the FTC’s 6(b) authority, which lets it conduct studies without any specific law enforcement purpose. “These eight firms advertise their use of AI and machine learning as part of the services they offer, often claiming they can use historical and real-time customer information to drive unique purchasing experiences,” an FTC official said on a call with reporters ahead of the announcement, adding that none of the firms issued orders have been accused of any wrongdoing. “What we’re trying to do is lift the hood on opaque practices that have the potential to profoundly reshape how consumers purchase goods and services. We want to make sure that surveillance pricing isn’t resulting in harm to certain communities, like women and rural consumers.” The companies are being asked to turn over information on: * Types of surveillance pricing products and services they’ve produced, developed, or licensed to a third party * Data sources used for each product or service * Who they’re offering surveillance pricing products and services to * How this impacts surveilled consumers and pricing On a call with reporters, an FTC official said a study is necessary because the extent to which businesses use surveillance pricing is currently unknown. Media reports suggest that companies across a wide variety of sectors — including grocery stores, restaurant chains, travel, and hospitality — are considering implementing surveillance pricing or have already done so. “The technology is there, the incentives are there, the data certainly is there to do this targeting,” the FTC official told reporters. “And now we actually see this industry of consultancies potentially offer to help companies personalize pricing, which gives us a strong reason to believe that this practice is likely to grow.”

articles.title: How AI companies are reckoning with elections
articles.summary: AI could play a prominent role in the 2024 US presidential election, and the companies behind it have each said how they plan to make sure their impact isn’t disastrous.
articles.body_text: The US is heading into its first presidential election since generative AI tools have gone mainstream. And the companies offering these tools — like Google, OpenAI, and Microsoft — have each made announcements about how they plan to handle the months leading up to it. This election season, we’ve already seen AI-generated images in ads and attempts to mislead voters with voice cloning. The potential harms from AI chatbots aren’t as visible in the public eye — yet, anyway. But chatbots are known to confidently provide made-up facts, including in responses to good-faith questions about basic voting information. In a high-stakes election, that could be disastrous. One plausible solution is to try to avoid election-related queries altogether. In December, Google announced that Gemini would simply refuse to answer election-related questions in the US, referring users to Google Search instead. Google spokesperson Christa Muldoon confirmed to The Verge via email the change is now rolling out globally. (Of course, that relies on the reliability of Google Search — something the company has been working on with an eye toward AI spam.) Muldoon said Google has “no plans” to lift these restrictions, which she said also “apply to all queries and outputs” generated by Gemini, not just text. Earlier this year, OpenAI said that ChatGPT would start referring users to CanIVote.org, generally considered one of the best online resources for local voting information. The company’s policy now forbids impersonating candidates or local governments using ChatGPT. It likewise prohibits using its tools for campaigning, lobbying, discouraging voting, or otherwise misrepresenting the voting process, under the updated rules. In a statement emailed to The Verge, Aravind Srinivas, CEO of the AI search company Perplexity, said Perplexity’s algorithms prioritize “reliable and reputable sources like news outlets” and that it always provides links so users can verify its output. In an email to The Verge, Microsoft representative Brian Gluckman says the company has rolled out updates to address concerns from a report last year about false election information provided by Copilot (formerly known as Bing). His email also pointed to the company’s blog post about combating abusive AI content as an example of the measures it’s applying, with provenance technology, bans for users who break the rules, and more. All of these companies’ responses (maybe Google’s most of all) are very different from how they’ve tended to approach elections with their other products. Google has used (and continues to use) Associated Press partnerships to bring factual election information to the top of search results and has tried to counter false claims about mail-in voting by using labels on YouTube. Other companies have made similar efforts — see Facebook’s voter registration links and Twitter’s anti-misinformation banner. Yet major events like the US presidential election seem like a real opportunity to prove whether AI chatbots are actually a useful shortcut to legitimate information. I asked a couple of Texas voting questions of some chatbots to get an idea of their usefulness. OpenAI’s ChatGPT 4 was able to correctly list the seven different forms of valid ID for voters, and it also identified that the next significant election is the primary runoff election on May 28th. Perplexity AI answered those questions correctly as well, linking multiple sources at the top. Copilot got its answers right and even did one better by telling me what my options were if I didn’t have any of the seven forms of ID. (ChatGPT also coughed up this addendum on a second try). Gemini just referred me to Google Search, which got me the right answers about ID, but when I asked for the date of next election, an out-of-date box at the top referred me to the March 5th primary. Many of the companies working on AI have made various commitments to prevent or mitigate the intentional misuse of their products. Microsoft says it will work with candidates and political parties to curtail election misinformation. The company has also started releasing what it says will be regular reports on foreign influences in key elections — its first such threat analysis came in November. Google says it will digitally watermark images created with its products using DeepMind’s SynthID. OpenAI and Microsoft have both announced that they would use the Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity’s (C2PA) digital credentials to denote AI-generated images with a CR symbol. But each company has said that these approaches aren’t enough. One way Microsoft plans to account for that is through its website that lets political candidates report deepfakes. Stability AI, which owns the Stable Diffusion image generator, updated its policies recently to ban using its product for “fraud or the creation or promotion of disinformation.” Midjourney told Reuters last week that “updates related specifically to the upcoming U.S. election are coming soon.” Its image generator performed the worst when it came to making misleading images, according to a Center for Countering Digital Hate report published last week. Meta announced in November of last year that it would require political advertisers to disclose if they used “AI or other digital techniques” to create ads published on its platforms. The company has also banned the use of its generative AI tools by political campaigns and groups. [Image: The “Seven Principle Goals” of the AI Elections accord. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/25332126/Screenshot_2024_03_12_at_11.21.50_AM.png?quality=90&strip=all] Several companies, including all of the ones above, signed an accord last month, promising to create new ways to mitigate the deceptive use of AI in elections. The companies agreed on seven “principle goals,” like research and deployment of prevention methods, giving provenance for content (such as with C2PA or SynthID-style watermarking), improving their AI detection capabilities, and collectively evaluating and learning from the effects of misleading AI-generated content. In January, two companies in Texas cloned President Biden’s voice to discourage voting in the New Hampshire primary. It won’t be the last time generative AI makes an unwanted appearance in this election cycle. As the 2024 race heats up, we’ll surely see these companies tested on the safeguards they’ve built and the commitments they’ve made. articles.title: Inside Facebook’s election war room
articles.summary: In a Menlo Park conference room, a global effort to fight misinformation comes together
articles.body_text: Information war, meet the war room. Facebook on Wednesday briefed reporters on its latest efforts to uncover nefarious uses of the platform during election season, offering a tour of the large conference room where dozens of employees are monitoring events around the clock. “We know when it comes to an elections, every moment counts,” said Samidh Chakrabarti, head of civic engagement at Facebook, who oversees the war room. “So if there are late-breaking issues we see on the platform, we need to be able to detect and respond to them in real time, as quickly as possible.” On one hand, the war room is just one of many conference rooms in MPK 20, the company’s Menlo Park, CA headquarters. But it’s larger than average, and has been stuffed with people and electronics equipment. There are desks for 24 people, and the room is ringed with 17 screens, each of which highlights a different stream of information Facebook is monitoring. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/13289699/T6B3ly8w.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] Employees look for suspicious spikes in spam and hate speech, in some cases using custom software built for the purpose. They look for efforts at voter suppression, such as falsely telling people that lines are long or that the election has been delayed. (The team recently uncovered one such hoax claiming that the Brazilian election date had been delayed a day due to protests, and swiftly removed the offending posts.) Sign up for The Interface Get The Verge’s daily newsletter about social networks and democracy the night before everyone else does. Sign up Other employees use CrowdTangle, a company acquired by Facebook that monitors the viral spread of articles across platforms, to detect which articles are trending on Facebook, Instagram, Twitter, and Reddit. All told, representatives from 20 teams have people in the war room, representing 20,000 global employees working on safety and security. The teams include threat intelligence, data science, engineering, research, operations, legal, policy, communications, and representatives from Facebook-owned WhatsApp and Instagram. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/13289701/ygMhHSnw.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] If anyone finds a problem, they escalate it to a specialist, who can then route it to the appropriate decision-maker. Facebook has also given state attorneys general and other elected officials a way to reach the war room quickly to report voter suppression and other suspicious activity. If the room is new, the work is not: Facebook teams have been working to fight misinformation in a coordinated way since 2016. The decision to bring them all together into a single room was made in the hopes that it would let them make decisions faster. “When every moment counts, then decision-making needs to be fast,” Chakrabarti sayd. “There’s no substitute for face to face, in-room interaction. so we felt [the need for] this physical war room to be able to coordinate teams.” On the day we visited, the room was decorated with a mix of American and Brazilian flags, in a nod to the next two elections that are being watched in the war room. It’s a fraught time: last week, Facebook removed 559 pages and 251 accounts in the United States for using fake identities and coordinating information campaigns. Meanwhile, Brazilian researchers today published the results of a study that examined the most-shared images in popular public WhatsApp chats and found that many of them contained misinformation: > From a sample of more than 100,000 political images that circulated in those 347 groups, we selected the 50 most widely shared. They were reviewed by Agência Lupa, which is Brazil’s leading fact-checking platform. Eight of those 50 photos and images were considered completely false; 16 were real pictures but used out of their original context or related to distorted data; four were unsubstantiated claims, not based on a trustworthy public source. This means that 56 percent of the most-shared images were misleading. Only 8 percent of the 50 most widely shared images were considered fully truthful. Facebook wouldn’t commit to keeping the war room open over forever. But with multiple elections taking place around the world each year, the company plans to keep it open for the foreseeable future. “This is going to be a constant arms race,” said Katie Harbath, Facebook’s global politics and government outreach director. “This is our new normal. Bad actors are going to get more sophisticated in what they’re doing, and we’re going to have to get more sophisticated in trying to catch them.”

articles.title: Norsk ilska mot Trump: ”Svek”
articles.summary: Trumps Ukrainapolitik kostar ukrainska liv. Det anser norske toppolitikern Peter Frølich. ”Det är ett svek mot den västliga alliansen”, säger Frølich.
articles.body_text: Trumps Ukrainapolitik kostar ukrainska liv. Det anser norske toppolitikern Peter Frølich – och det gör honom ”så förbannad”. – Det är ett svek mot den västliga alliansen, säger Frølich till norska Dagbladet . Ljuduppspelningen är AI-genererad. Felaktigheter kan förekomma. Peter Frølich är ordförande för norska riksdagen Stortingets utrikes- och försvarsutskott. Tillfrågad om han tror det snart blir fred i Ukraina svarar han ”nej” och pekar ut Vladimir Putin som det största hindret. – Ryssland kan inte tillåtas tillbaka in i världssamfundets värme förrän de har dragit sig tillbaka och respekterat de ursprungliga gränserna. Det är därför jag blir så förbannad när jag hör om hur amerikanerna planerar stora affärsuppgörelser och häver sanktionerna, säger Frølich. President Donald Trump har nyligen sagt att ”Ryssland överlag betett sig ganska rimligt mot Ukraina” och påstått att ukrainske presidenten Volodymyr Zelenskyj ”inte vill avsluta kriget”. – Jag tycker att Zelenskyj är svårare att ha att göra med än Putin, sade Trump till tv-kanalen Newsmax nyligen. Zelenskyj har sagt att han känt sig ”förrådd” av Trump. Frølich, som kallar sig själv ”en gammal USA-vän”, anklagar Trump för att ha ”brutit mot grundläggande gränser för anständighet” och ”aktivt gett stöd till den ryska krigsmaskinen”. – När det gäller Donald Trump har bägaren svämmat över. Gränsen är sedan länge nådd, säger Frølich. Från ukrainskt håll har man lyft den senaste tidens hastighetsrestriktioner i Elon Musks satellitsystem Starlink, som landet är beroende av för sitt försvar, och att man behöver få många fler robotar till Patriot-systemen av USA för att bekämpa den ryska invasionen. Frølich anser att Trumps beslut får direkta konsekvenser vid fronten och ”leder till dödsfall bland ukrainska civila och soldater”.

articles.title: Skräcken på lyxkryssning – strandats
articles.summary: Det som skulle bli en drömresa blev en mardröm. Nu är hundratals passagerare på en lyxkryssning strandsatta i ett främmande land.
articles.body_text: Det som skulle bli en drömresa blev en mardröm. Kryssningsföretaget har inte längre råd med bränslet. Nu är hundratals passagerare på en lyxkryssning strandsatta i ett främmande land, skriver New York Post . Ljuduppspelningen är AI-genererad. Felaktigheter kan förekomma. Kryssningsfartyget Odyssey, som ägs av Florida-baserade Villa Vie Residences, påbörjade för två år sedan en treårig jordenruntresa. Priserna för hytterna sträckte sig från 1,3 miljoner till 4,4 miljoner kronor, plus månadsavgifter på 20 000 till 100 000 kronor, för vad som utlovades som en resa till sju kontinenter med besök på över 400 resmål. Fartyget, som har en kapacitet på 650 personer, har haft 203 passagerare ombord tillsammans med 156 besättningsmedlemmar, enligt tjänstemän. Men ett orosmoment på resan på senare tid har varit de ökande bränslepriserna till följd av det skakiga läget i Mellanöstern. Passagerarna Lanette Canen och Johan Bodin sade att de upprepade gånger fått höra att kryssningsföretaget höll på att få slut på pengar. ”Vi har inte kunnat fortsätta bära de resulterande rörelseförlusterna”, skriver Villa Vie Residences i ett uttalande som publicerades på tisdagen. I samband med detta ska passagerarna ha fått följande meddelande: ”Tyvärr kunde vi inte säkra det bränsle som krävdes för att fortsätta färden. Som ett resultat av detta kommer Odyssey att tillfälligt tas ur trafik i eftermiddag, med besättningen kvar ombord för att underhålla fartyget och dess viktiga system. Alla passagerare måste gå i land senast klockan 14 i dag.” Nu ligger fartyget förtöjt i den kambodjanska hamnen Sihanoukville och passagerarna är strandsatta. Passageraren Randy Cassingham uppgav att företaget ”inte har gjort någonting alls för att hjälpa” passagerare att hitta boende och ”absolut inte erbjudit sig att betala för vårt boende”.

articles.title: S-toppen om låsta läget i regeringsbildningen: ”Ängslighet”

Socialdemokraterna har ett särskilt ansvar. – Det parti som har tänkt ta den yttersta posten har alltid ett ansvar i en förhandling att försöka få alla parter till bordet, säger hon till Svenska Dagbladet.

Socialdemokraterna har ett särskilt ansvar. – Det parti som har tänkt ta den yttersta posten har alltid ett ansvar i en förhandling att försöka få alla parter till bordet, säger hon till Svenska Dagbladet. Ljuduppspelningen är AI-genererad. Felaktigheter kan förekomma. Både S-ledaren Magdalena Andersson och C-ledaren Elisabeth Thand Ringqvist har misslyckats med sina sonderingsförsök. Just nu har ingen partiledare sonderingsuppdraget. Katrin Stjernfeldt Jammeh, kommunstyrelsens ordförande i Malmö, tycker att det är ”olyckligt” att regeringsbildningen tar så lång tid. Hon säger till SvD att hon vill se en ”handlingskraftig regering” som ”får hela mandatperioden på sig att styra, prioritera och satsa”. – Jag tycker att det är beklagligt att man inte har fått till processen så att man får fram en budget i tid till exempel, säger Stjernfeldt Jammeh till tidningen. Med en stram övergångsbudget, som troligen kommer att antas av riksdagen i november, kan många kommuner och regioner som hoppats på höjda statsbidrag i stället tvingas till olika neddragningar, enligt Stjernfeldt Jammeh. I Malmö styr Socialdemokraterna , Miljöpartiet och Vänsterpartiet ihop. Stjernfeldt Jammeh svarar varken ja eller nej på SvD:s fråga om hon tycker att Vänsterpartiet är redo för att sitta med i regeringen, utan säger att hon ”överlåter” diskussionen till partiledningen. Hon konstaterar dock att Vänsterpartiet ”är med och styr runtom i landet” och säger att det finns ”många frågor” där Socialdemokraterna och Vänsterpartiet ”tycker politiskt väldigt lika”.

articles.title: Trodde hon var förkyld – dog i svenskparadis
articles.summary: Rachel Weston trodde hon blivit förkyld under semestern på turistön. Sedan kollapsade 42-åringen och dog.
articles.body_text: Rachel Weston trodde hon blivit förkyld under semestern på turistön. Sedan kollapsade 42-åringen och dog, skriver Manchester Evening News . ”Min värld vändes helt upp och ner”, skriver Rachels make Mark. Ljuduppspelningen är AI-genererad. Felaktigheter kan förekomma. 42-åriga brittiskan Rachel Weston reste i början av månaden till semesterön Lanzarote tillsammans med maken Mark och två vänner. När Rachel plötsligt började må dåligt trodde hon först att hon blivit förkyld. Men när hennes hälsotillstånd försämrades bestämde sig paret för att boka ett sista minuten-flyg hem till följande dag. Då kollapsade Rachel inne på sitt hotellrum. Hennes liv kunde inte räddas och hon dödförklarades på platsen. Ingen dödsorsak har offentliggjorts. ”Min värld vändes helt upp och ner med den plötsliga och hjärtskärande förlusten av min underbara fru Rachel medan vi var på semester. Rachel och jag var tillsammans i elva år och en dag. Vi var tyvärr bara gifta i två av de åren, men varje dag var full av kärlek, skratt och gemenskap”, skriver Mark. Rachel beskrevs av maken som ”hemmets absoluta hjärta”. ”Att förlora henne så oväntat är en riktig mardröm. Det är en enorm börda att bära”, skriver Mark. Detta är en nyhetsartikel. articles.title: Nya uppgifterna chockar experter

articles.body_text: Personalen använde omkring tio nålar och kämpade i nästan en timme med att hitta en fungerande ven. Till slut fick Christa Pike två doser av ett dödligt preparat – men överlevde. Den 30 september skulle Christa Pike , 50, avrättas i den amerikanska delstaten Tennessee. Hon hade dömts till döden för mordet på klasskamraten Colleen Slemmer 1995, då hon själv var 18 år. Men avrättningen gick inte som planerat. Trots två doser av preparatet pentobarbital överlevde hon. Nu har Pikes advokat Randy Spivey, som själv var på plats i avrättningskammaren, lämnat in en detaljerad redogörelse för avrättningsförsöket till domstol. Här är några av de viktigaste uppgifterna: 18.21: Fängelsepersonal hämtar Christa Pike från hennes cell. Hon spänns fast på en bår och förs till avrättningskammaren. 18.34: Personalen börjar leta efter fungerande vener i Pikes armar. articles.summary: Donald Trump åkte ända till Alaska för att öka Dan Sullivans chanser att vinna det viktiga senatvalet. Nu ligger han bakom en stämning mot – Dan Sullivan.
articles.body_text: Donald Trump åkte ända till Alaska för att öka Dan Sullivans chanser att vinna det viktiga senatvalet. Nu ligger han bakom en stämning mot – Dan Sullivan. Sullivan medvetet ställts upp för att förvirra väljare och skada den sittande senatorn Dan S. Sullivan. Trump har fått justitiedepartementet att stämma Alaska för att stoppa certifieringen av valresultatet om kandidaten blir kvar på valsedeln. Det har varit en snackis ända sen primärvalet i somras. ”Den riktiga” Dan Sullivan, med initialen S, är republikan och sittande senator. Han blev bara tvåa i primärvalet efter demokraten Mary Peltola – något som inte bara lär ha haft med Peltolas budskap att göra, utan också med att det var en till Dan Sullivan på valsedeln: den pensionerade läraren Dan J Sullivan. Dan J Sullivan säger att han ”ändå hade tid över” för att försöka bli senator. Bland många republikaner i Alaska är Dan J nu ett rött skynke, och han kallas ”Decoy Dan” – villospåret. När Donald Trump i mitten av månaden var i Wasilla i Alaska och kampanjade för Dan S Sullivan (den sittande senatorn, alltså), gick han till angrepp mot Dan J Sullivan och demokraterna.

articles.summary: Vännerna mekade med en fyrhjuling när det plötsligt började brinna i garaget. – Vi fick lite panik och försökte släcka det. Men det gick inte, så då försökte vi ta oss ut så snabbt det gick, berättar 13-årige Albin Ottosson.
articles.body_text: Vännerna mekade med en fyrhjuling när det plötsligt började brinna i garaget. – Vi fick lite panik och försökte släcka det. Kompisgänget hade precis fått höstlov och mekade med en fyrhjuling i en kompis garage i Fristad utanför Borås, som man gjort många gånger tidigare. Men plötsligt gick någonting fel och det började brinna inne i garaget . Ungdomarna insåg snabbt att de behövde ta sig ut. – Men vi fick först inte upp dörren, berättar Albin Ottosson, 13, som är en av dem som befann sig inne i garaget. Initiativet har kritiserats av andra politiska ledare och forskare. Diplomaten Jan Eliasson är positiv och anser att Norden bör ta en större roll i internationell medling. Han betonar att Europa behöver en egen röst i fredssamtalen. Samtidigt anser han att kontakten med Putin borde ha samordnats bättre och lyfter behovet till nordisk enighet och samarbete. Norges statsminister Jonas Gahr Støre och Finlands president Alexander Stubb hade ett cirka 90 minuter långt telefonsamtal med Rysslands president Vladimir Putin på tisdagsförmiddagen. Europeiska regeringschefer fick information om telefonsamtalet ungefär en timme innan det ägde rum. Kritiken kom snabbt. – Jag är mycket skeptisk. Det är inte koordinerat med oss andra, sa Danmarks statsminister Mette Frederiksen.
